group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 46-year-old man was sent in from the subacute rehabilitation wing of a long-term care facility where he has resided for the past three months following a mechanical fall that fractured his left tibial plateau; the nurse practitioner on duty noted that over the prior twenty-four hours he had developed fever, a deep productive cough yielding thick yellow-gray sputum, and rapid, shallow breathing that persisted even while he sat quietly in bed. The patient reports that the febrile sensation began the preceding evening, prompting staff to measure an oral temperature of 101.5 °F that responded only minimally to a single dose of 650 mg acetaminophen; overnight he experienced rigors and was unable to sleep flat because every attempt at reclining provoked a suffocating sensation. He denies chills at the moment of interview but endorses diffuse myalgia, pleuritic discomfort along the right posterior chest, diminished appetite, and one episode of non-bilious emesis after an intense coughing spell. His background is notable for compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis discovered six years ago during evaluation for persistent thrombocytopenia, for which he completed an antiviral course but still follows hepatology every four months; liver ultrasound three months earlier showed a nodular contour without ascites, and he has never required paracentesis or experienced hepatic encephalopathy. There is no known history of chronic kidney impairment, diabetes medication use, stroke, malignancy, or cardiomyopathy, and he last smoked cigarettes twelve years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure; alcohol intake was heavy in his twenties but has been abstinent since the cirrhosis diagnosis. Functional status prior to the recent fracture had been independent for all activities of daily living, though he required a cane for balance because of peripheral neuropathic changes from years of alcohol misuse. The nursing facility has not administered any antibiotics, intravenous fluids, or supplemental oxygen, electing instead to transfer him emergently so that baseline measurements would remain pristine. On arrival he was seated upright on the gurney, skin flushed and diaphoretic yet alert, oriented to person, place, date, and circumstance, answering questions coherently and following multistep commands without hesitation. Initial, untreated vital signs recorded an oral temperature of 101.5 °F, a regular peripheral pulse that staff counted at 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate an impressive 43 breaths per minute with visible intercostal retractions, and automated blood pressure 116/68 mm Hg confirmed manually; room-air finger-tip oximetry fluctuated between 86 % and 89 %. Capillary refill was brisk; sclerae were anicteric, and mild palmar erythema was present, findings unchanged from hepatology notes. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, extra sounds, or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination demonstrated coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the entire right middle and lower lung zones posteriorly, with resonant percussion throughout and no stony dullness or shifting dullness suggestive of free pleural fluid; the left lung transmitted vesicular sounds without adventitious noise. Abdomen was soft with a palpable but non-tender left-lobe liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no fluid wave, and normal bowel sounds. There was no pedal edema. Neurologic screening showed equal pupils, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all extremities limited only by the healing orthopedic injury, symmetric reflexes, and steady finger-to-nose testing. Point-of-care glucometry before placement of any lines read 126 mg/dL. Radial arterial blood sampled on room air within ten minutes of presentation revealed pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg, PaO₂ 61 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, consistent with a primary metabolic acidosis from presumed lactic accumulation and a superimposed respiratory alkalosis driven by tachypnea. A comprehensive metabolic panel drawn concurrently showed sodium 120 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, chloride 92 mEq/L, bicarbonate matching the blood gas, blood urea nitrogen 45 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, and AST/ALT mildly above baseline at 68/72 IU/L. Complete blood count yielded leukocytes 15.4 × 10⁹/L with 89 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 57 %, hemoglobin 19.0 g/dL, and platelets 104 × 10⁹/L, numbers consistent with his chronic portal hypertensive profile except for the elevated white count. Venous lactate returned at 3.2 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any pharmacologic or respiratory intervention depicted a dense consolidation occupying the entire right lower lobe with prominent air bronchograms, while both costophrenic angles remained sharp and the cardiac silhouette was normal in size. Electrocardiogram recorded sinus rhythm at 98 beats per minute with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Blood cultures from two separate peripheral sticks, a sputum Gram stain with culture, and rapid respiratory viral PCR panel were obtained prior to the completion of this note. Up to this point the patient had received no antipyretics beyond the earlier acetaminophen, no antibiotics, no intravenous crystalloids, no vasoactive agents, and no supplemental oxygen, ensuring that the physiological and laboratory values documented above represent his untreated state at initial presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: male age 46 → 46; nursing facility resident → 10.
- Comorbidities: cirrhosis qualifies as liver disease → 20. No reported malignancy, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, or chronic renal disease → 0 each.
- Examination: respiratory rate 43/min (≥30) → 20. Mentation normal → 0; systolic BP 116 (not <90 mm Hg) → 0; temperature 38.6°C (not <35 or ≥40°C) → 0; pulse 100 (not ≥125/min) → 0.
- Labs: arterial pH 7.25 (<7.35) → 30; BUN 45 (≥30 mg/dL) → 20; sodium 120 (<130 mEq/L) → 20. Glucose 126 (not ≥250 mg/dL) → 0; hematocrit 57% (not <30%) → 0.
- Oxygenation and imaging: using measured arterial PaO₂, 61 mm Hg does not meet the <60 threshold → 0. This calculation does not substitute the low pulse oximetry reading for the available arterial measurement. No pleural effusion → 0.
Total = 46 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 30 + 20 + 20 = 166 (risk class V).
Final answer: 166
